utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there were two preliminary matters to be raised by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The first matter relates to the next witness, Mr. Jeremy Bowen. He's a witness which we intend to use a number of videos during the direct examination. Last week during the recess the court interpreters, CLSS, very generously agreed to go through all of those and verify the transcripts of those videos. So the Prosecution is seeking leave to -- not to play the videos twice in court. We believe that will expedite the examination. That's the first matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they have been verified and if there's no objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber grants your request to proceed as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. The second matter, Your Honours, relates to Witness RM280. Yesterday the Chamber entered a decision denying the Prosecution application to tender that evidence 92 bis. It may help the Chamber to recall that this witness relates to the Skorpion video. In the Chamber's decision, the Chamber says: "Invites the Prosecution to present Witness RM280 as a viva voce witness or under Rule 92 ter of the Rules." The Prosecution would like to call the witness as a 92 ter witness and wants to verify with the Chamber that it -- the Prosecution does not have to file a 92 ter application. The Prosecution would tender the same material that it had tendered under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence that it's mainly a matter of formality?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection. We talked about this with the other side prior to the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber grants your request. No separate 92 ter motion has to be filed. We'll just accept this as an oral application.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, I did understand that you would finish your cross-examination during the first session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask you something regarding your testimony before the International Court of Justice. Is it true that in that case you acted on behalf of the interests of the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was called as an expert witness by the plaintiffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are aware that with regard to these proceedings the Serbian representatives in the joint organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not provided their consent?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not privy to the procedural background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, and I'm addressing you as well, Mr. Riedlmayer, the previous question was whether: "It is true that in that case you acted on behalf of the interests of the Bosnian Muslims." Your answer was: "Yes, I was called as an expert witness by the plaintiffs."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is inconsistent to the extent that a witness is a witness of truth and not -- you're not acting on behalf of the interest of the Bosnian Muslims. I do not know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was acting on behalf of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there for a second [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are again using "acting on behalf of," whereas the Chamber understands a witness or an expert witness not to act on behalf of the party that called that witness, but once being called by that witness acts in order to give testimony of the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is something different from acting on behalf of a party. When you said: "Yes, I was called as an expert witness by the plaintiffs," do I properly understand that your commitment was to perform your duty as an expert witness rather than to act on behalf of one of the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please excuse the sloppy phrasing. In fact, I was an expert witness, and as such testified in court to the best of my knowledge. But it was the plaintiffs who called me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear. Mr. Lukic, you more or less putting this question to someone who may not be that much involved in legal matters is at least asking perhaps for confusion. Then your second question - and let me look at that for one second - you referred I think in your second question -- yes, had not provided a consent. May I take it that they had not provided their consent to do what? To bring the case before the ICJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we understand it. But to give consent could be in any respect. Please proceed I -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, my colleagues informed me - although I didn't notice it myself being focused on what I was doing - that Mr. Mladic communicated to the public gallery in an unacceptable way. He's hereby warned that he should not do that again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, is it true that in some of your papers you had claimed that Serb nationalists in Republika Srpska passed anti-racial laws prohibiting the mixture of genes, which means that every non-Serb who would marry a Serbian woman or engage in sexual intercourse with a Serbian woman would be deemed to have committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that has come up in previous cross-examinations. It is true that in 1993, while the war was still going on, I wrote a short pamphlet on a web site which reflected a news report to this effect. I later learned that this was not true, that in fact, like so many news reports, it misstated the actual situation. It is true, as has come out since the war, that people in mixed marriages were encouraged to leave; but it is not true that mixed marriages were prohibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your question was whether the witness had claimed this and this and this. Now, for the -- it certainly would assist the Chamber in order to better assess the testimony of the witness whether there was a personal claim or whether there was just a reference to a -- in that pamphlet to reports given by others. So it certainly would assist the Chamber to see what personal commitment was given by the witness on that, but you have not put it to the witness. The Chamber is unaware of the pamphlet and the content of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, you heard His Honour Orie. Can you explain what kind of pamphlet was that and what was your role in writing the same?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a posting on a web site which has long since vanished from the web, but I believe you can probably find a copy of it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more now?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It was called: A short history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was seven pages long. It was not a formal publication, had no footnotes and no references, and it dealt with the war only in its last page or so. Subsequently I have published formal publications that deal with the same subject which have gone through a proper editing process and which are properly sourced. I stand by those. They are listed on my CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you put that -- put a claim, as was part of the question -- did you at least present it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as being a fact or did you say: Well, I read this and this and this in that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I no longer remember the exact phrasing, but given that it was not a formal paper, nothing was footnoted according to source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I think back, I don't know whether I said "alleged" or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, okay, so then we don't know at this moment whether or not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 20 years ago, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was 20 years ago. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You yourself said that it was in 1993, which means while the war was going on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that, for example, you had stated that Serbs persecuted both the gypsies and the Jews in the papers that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that. Gypsies, yes, but I -- what it refers to is that Jewish heritage was also damaged in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D1334, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's an excerpt from this short paper entitled: The brief history of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I don't know that I have an objection, but I just observe this wasn't on the -- I don't think this was on the exhibit list we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, we've -- I'm looking at the video on the screen which doesn't match --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But I'd withdraw my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document is on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the list. Please think about it before you raise, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we need page 8, last paragraph and last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read so we have it in the transcript: "The dwindling number of non-Serb inhabitants remaining in the zones under Serb control have been barred from employment in the public sector and are required to display white flags on their places of residence. Denied police protection by the nationalist authorities, non-Serbs (Muslims, Croats, Gypsies, and Jews) remaining in Banja Luka and other occupied Bosnian towns have been subjected to vicious attacks, including robbery, murder, and rape, carried out with impunity in broad daylight." [Interpretation] Would you agree with me that this was not only about the destruction of the cultural heritage, but that you also asserted that Serbs were attacking Jews as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears I did and I disavow it. I no longer believe that; at the time I must have. It was 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in fact you personally were involved in the propaganda war against the Serbs in this manner by attempting to compare them with the German Nazis and the fascists of Italy?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a loaded question. I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's perhaps start with the factual part, that is, whether you compared them with fascist regimes of the past. That's a factual question. The other one --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is whether you played a role in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to review the document again to see whether I exactly said that, but I do -- I do believe that I characterised the ideology of extreme nationalism as analogous to the same ideologies during World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, was your question focused on this document or was it a more general sense focused on what the witness expressed as his opinion not necessarily in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily only in this document. We saw that his writing before was about that -- those laws allegedly forbidding marriages between Serbs and others. And based on this document as well, where he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you are referring to other documents, again earlier I said I would like to have a look at that pamphlet. If you would have said: You'll see it in a minute that would have clarified matters clearly. Now, for the other sources will we see that as well, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just spoke to Mr. Traldi this morning. We both tried to locate something from Seselj trial and it's not easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since he never mentions any numbers of the documents or exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay so --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have the trace from the first part, I have the trace in the transcript, and for this one I have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to make sure that you still have your train of thought, in response to a question by Judge Orie you referred to the witness alleging forbidden marriages by the Serbs with others. The question you were talking about was not about marriages any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were talking about comparison with extreme nationalists and fascists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You publicly characterised the radical party of Dr. Vojislav Seselj as being a fascist party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This also came up in the cross-examination in the Seselj case. Back about a few months before that case a friend had written to me, worrying that the former Yugoslavia was sliding back into war, the rhetoric was escalating, so I wrote him back an elaborate reply and I think as part of the reply I pointed out that if the Serbian election went to the Radicals, that it would be a bad thing. And in that, I characterised the ideology of the Radical party as neo-fascist. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this a private correspondence or was it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a private correspondence, but then he posted it on his blog. It's the nature of the Internet, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You presented your personal views in that letter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was an informal analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina you urged --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have trouble hearing --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that the Muslims' embargo be lifted.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a technical problem. Mr. Riedlmayer has difficulties in hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I turned up the volume. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's all right now. Could you please repeat your question now, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct that during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina you personally advocated the arming of the Muslims, the lifting of the embargo on arms imports into Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, and -- I believe this refers to something that had come up in cross-examination. In the summer of 1995 I was a signatory to an open letter to the Clinton administration urging the lifting of the arms embargo, in which I argued that under the United Nations Charters, Chapter 7, Article 51, Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a member state of the United Nations, retained the right for self-defence. And the article further says that it has the right to do so until the Security Council can take effective measures to restore peace and security. By the summer of 1995 it seemed clear to me that, in fact, the United Nations had not succeeded in restoring peace and security. So I think it was a reasonable view to defend.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you have had a pro-Muslim/anti-Serb leanings?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, again, that's a loaded question. I am not pro-Muslim or anti-Serb. I am in favour of a civic Bosnia-Herzegovina and do not believe in ethnic partitions. However, I'm not a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina so it's obviously not up to me to determine its form of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mostar is not part of the indictment; however, is it correct that you testified when you testified before the International Court of Justice, that the Muslim -- the mosques in the city were destroyed by the Serbs during the siege of the town. Would you still stand by what you said then?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of my sworn testimony in the Seselj case as well. The first siege of Mostar from April through June of 1992 by the Yugoslav national army in fact - as was determined among others by the rapporteur for the Council of Europe - did damage 11 out of 12 mosques in Mostar, and the second siege by Croat forces did not begin until the following spring and only compounded the damage in most cases. So I think it's fact; it's not something that is open to question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And regarding the old bridge in Mostar, did you -- you claimed that the JNA destroyed it and would you still stand by that position today?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never claimed that the JNA destroyed the bridge. It did damage the bridge. There were a number of impacts on the bridge itself and the two medieval towers on either side of the bridge were seriously damaged. The bridge however was brought down in September -- I'm sorry in November of 1993 by the Bosnian Croat siege. But neither in my testimony before the ICJ nor in my testimony in the Seselj trial did I claim that the destruction of the bridge was solely the work of the Yugoslav national army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D1332 in the e-court, please. It's transcript from Seselj trial from May 28, 2008, and we need page 12 in the e-court and it should correspond to page 7494 of the Seselj transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 11 you said in your response, and I quote: "With regard to the Old Bridge, I spoke about it in some detail during that direct examination, the kind of damage that was sustained by it, and indeed it is true it was damaged in the JNA siege and it was the main casualty of the 1993-1994 Croat siege of the old city of Mostar." [Interpretation] When you say that you know that it was the JNA that damaged the bridge, could you tell us, according to what you know, what this damage exactly was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness just told us before you called this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but he didn't specify what were the damages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He said the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the JNA damaged the points -- all points on either side of the bridge and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said a few hits and it damaged the -- destroyed the bridge. So therefore, if you have any further questions, please ask for further details, but not again in this general way. By the way, Mr. Lukic, if the witness in the quote you gave said: I spoke about it in some detail during the direct examination, then of course we would have to see the direct examination to know what details were -- the witness was referring to; otherwise, it's impossible for this Chamber to further assess what this testimony exactly is about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The damage which, according to you, was inflicted by the JNA, was that of a structural nature and did it threaten the stability of the bridge or did traffic proceed unhindered over the -- across the bridge until it was ultimately destroyed by the Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the bridge was not one that carried traffic. It's entirely used by pass -- pedestrians. Secondly, the damage to the bridge I evaluated from photographs. I'm not privy to what the internal structure is and how it might have been affected. The photographs show impacts on the main arch of the bridge, destroying parts of the parapet, and the stonework. The larger damage was to the two medieval towers that support either end of the bridge. As for the passenger traffic, the pedestrian traffic continuing unimpeded. In fact, I have photographs showing the bridge in 1992 which have corrugated iron sheeting on sort of a haphazard framework put over the bridge structure and people scurrying underneath to cross. So presumably it was dangerous to cross. These are by international news photographers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you hear that it was actually dangerous to cross the bridge because of the fighting between the Muslims and Croats and that's why it was a danger for the pedestrian traffic moving across the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, during the April-June 1992 siege of Mostar by the JNA, there was no fighting between Muslims and Croats. It did not begin until spring the following year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Going over the material, did you ever come across a statement or see a document in which General Ratko Mladic urged the destruction of Muslim cultural monuments or places of worship?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the preparation of my report, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that the head of the Serbian Orthodox church, Patriarch Pavle, addressed the public a number of times, urging restraint from destroying the religious facilities of the other ethnic groups and communities?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. These are all my questions to you and I complete my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Thank you. Mr. Traldi, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I'm going to ask you about a small number of the sites Mr. Lukic asked you about. Regarding Brisevo Mr. Lukic suggested to you that you had opined Serb -- sorry that Seselj's paramilitaries were responsible for the attack on Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 1D01331, page 53, please. Could we have the next page actually. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the top we see Mr. Seselj introducing this text and then in the next paragraph when he reads it he says: "Towards the end of the text, you go on to say, it is line 5 from the bottom, that the Bosnian Serb Army and Seselj's paramilitaries cleansed at enormous human cost this place Brisevo." Does that refresh your recollection as to what you wrote in that text?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 13413, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And while that comes up, is that -- is what you wrote there that the Bosnian Serb army was involved consistent with the information you received beforehand and an opinion you still hold today?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The information I had was from the parish priest who was in charge and who had been in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Moving south, Mr. Lukic asked you about the destruction of mosques in Banja Luka. Have you studied those mosques?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. They were dealt with within some of my other reports for other cases in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if you could take a moment and study the map on the screen, does it accurately set out the Banja Luka mosques?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. There were a total of 16 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did any mosques in Banja Luka survive the war undamaged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: None did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 13413. I note for the record that 65 ter also includes the Bosnia-wide map we used yesterday. For the record, we have also provided the Chamber a CD of a colour version of that map because the file size of the colour version is too large for e-court, and we've uploaded a surrogate sheet associated with that CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any objections against the admission of this document and the map attached to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just looking, is that from the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- one of the documents cited in his report, 65 ter 13413.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, yesterday I think we dealt with the same number that was already the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, I hadn't tendered it at the time, though, Your Honour, so I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are tendering that now. Madam Registrar, 65 ter 13413 receives number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P2505, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2505 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And regarding the Banja Luka mosques, I'd refer Your Honours as well to the evidence of RM99, which has been tendered pursuant to Rule 92 quater and to Exhibit P358, page 156. Could we next have 65 ter 17414, page 5 in the English and 7 in the B/C/S, below what will be a number 4. This document wasn't on the initial list for the witness but arises out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, one additional question in relation to 13413. All the text on it, is there an English translation available for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll check over the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Moving just west of Banja Luka, sir, Mr. Lukic suggested to you that where mosques were dynamited, that meant civilians had been responsible. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This document reads in pertinent part that: "Mosques in Sehovci, Trnova and Skucani Vakuf and a Catholic church in Stara Rijeka have been blown up." It continues: "Some of these 'experts' and perpetrators, some of whom are officers ..." and says that: " ... cases involving explosives and mines came from army depots and combat sets of subordinate units." Is that your -- is that consistent with your understanding that the destruction of mosques with explosives is consistent with destruction by the military?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. I visited all of these sites as well and they show every sign of having been destroyed by large amounts of explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17414 receives number P2506, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on admission, Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Traldi, you introduced the document by saying this document reads, but what is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could turn to the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's a report from, I believe, CSB Banja Luka. And you can see that in the top left on the B/C/S there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P2506 is admitted into evidence. Could I urge the parties always if they take a quote from a document, to at least inform the Chamber whether it's a novel, whether it's a historical document, whether it's -- whatever it is because text in itself needs sometimes context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next, sir, Mr. Lukic referred to your Krajisnik testimony about the Aladza mosque and at temporary transcript pages 72 and 73 yesterday, he suggested that that destruction was not related to the authorities. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is the destruction of the Aladza mosque consistent with what happened to the other mosques in Foca?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Every other mosque in Foca was also destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in your view, is the destruction of that mosque best understood in isolation or in context of what you've just described?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe it was an isolated incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Lukic asked you yesterday at temporary transcript page 78 if you had ever seen a document which suggested that the destruction of mosques was part of a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 19209. Mr. President, this is an order from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, just for the record you referred to the pages of yesterday's transcript, which of course does appear -- I see that the Aladza mosque has been introduced in what is now page 17955 of yesterday's transcript, where Mr. Lukic took the witness to paragraph 50 of his report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think yesterday's transcript must just have been updated during the session today with the final pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you for it. We know that that happens the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this document, sir, as you'll see, is labelled with the Drina Corps command in the top left. And in the middle, below the word "order" it says: "To use mechanical equipment of the engineering company in your brigade and start immediately with removal of remains of the destroyed mosque in Konjevic Polje." In point 2 it says: "The remains of the mosque are to be dumped at the closest site for disposal of waste material." Do you connect that to events you're familiar with from your studies?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mosque at Konjevic Polje was covered in my expert report for the Milosevic trial and also for the Karadzic trial, I believe. And the mosque was completely destroyed and the only thing left was the foundations. I believe I submitted a picture of the foundations which were still visible along the tall grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tender this document as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P2507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, there are three related documents relevant to the logistics of carrying out the task and the requisition of fuel for it. I'd like to just address those three through the bar table as well if there's no objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, similar documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I propose, since the witness won't have anything additional to say about them, just providing Mr. Lukic with the numbers over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we'll hear from you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two video-clips remaining, so I think we'll go very slightly past the break and I wonder if it might be simplest to take the break just a couple of minutes early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break a little bit early. Could I ask the usher to escort Mr. Riedlmayer out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start. We had to deal with an urgent matter which took us more time than we expected. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I said, I have two clips remaining. The first is from the Srebrenica trial video, P1147. I believe translation of the video has been confirmed and so we'll only need to play it once. And if we can start at 38 minutes, 6 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We only have one transcript, not two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been informed the interpreters have only one transcript. That, of course, is for the other video. This video the transcript's on the screen and I've been told the subtitles are visible to them. I apologise if I'd misunderstood that, but that's what I'd been informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're inviting the interpreters to use the verified subtitling as ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think just clarifying further, I would invite them to do that, but we I think don't always rely on the booth for -- to read the subtitles since they've already been confirmed and are part of evidence and so I'd ask the witness to look at this as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is acceptable for the various booths.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The only concern is that the subtitles are removed too quickly sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then what we perhaps should do, play it in portions or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- I think if the witness is comfortable reading the subtitles and the other Anglophones in the room are also comfortable reading the subtitles then we could work on that basis, as I believe we have before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I was consulting with one of my colleagues, so I missed -- I took off my headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your microphone's on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, in order to have a complete transcript, we need words spoken which are then transcribed. We can't just rely on text written as subtitles on the video. I suggest the following, that we re-start playing the video but that we take -- I take it that Ms. Stewart is in charge of it being played -- and that we stop now and then for just a few seconds so that interpreters and transcription can follow us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Traldi, you were on your feet before. I missed what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise. I am -- I'm being informed that we haven't previously had the booth interpret portions of this video while it was being played, and I wonder if I might give the transcript pages from the transcript that's been admitted as an alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that we have -- in the previous testimony of the witness portions of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For instance, in the testimony of expert Butler, I think at T16415, a portion of this was played and my recollection is that there wasn't interpretation over the video. We simply used the video. Now, it hasn't been played with one of my witnesses before, so Your Honour's memory may be more specific than mine, but my understanding is that's how we proceeded in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this video already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour, this is P1147 -- this is a portion of P1147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we give it a try to see whether we could have a complete transcript. If we fail to do that, then we would still -- is it a long portion you are playing now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's approximately three minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately three minutes. Then I suggest that we stop after every 20 or 25 seconds and see whether we are on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That works for me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If it works for Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and if it works for the interpreters and for the transcriber. Let's give it a try.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Under aviation and under air force strikes towards -- and to tell you frankly, cards on the table, I went on the asphalt road Jadar, Kozlje, Rajine, Petrica and saw a minaret reaching the sky. I think already this morning it has been flattened, it should have been this morning. Trust me, I only looked towards our church spire and some wish of mine carried me on to get to that point as soon as possible. Because I grew up there. And believe me, in my documents it says Easter 1995, even officially it is called differently in our documents, but I wrote it down in my documents that this is Easter. Why Easter, because it should have been Easter 1993 because Easter is eternal, meaning we met it. "On my way to Srebrenica I saw the most Turkish mosque you can imagine, a very Turkish mosque, and I guess our enemies wanted it to be higher than the church and therefore they took down half of our bell-tower to make the minaret a bit higher. However, I was asked this morning: 'General, has this famous mosque been finished?' I told them: 'I think that they finished it this morning.' So I said that it was 'finished' this morning. Well, let me tell you some more, the town as such was not crowded with residents as they said over whose ever Motorolas. "No, no, no, it was not like that. They had fantastic weaponry in Motorolas and scared gullible Serbs, you know. It is best to listen to the Turks as little as possible and one should not listen to some of the less good Serbs either. Simply, take the sword in your hand and go ahead! Our army started out powerfully towards Potocari. Yesterday evening forces were introduced from the police force in Bratunac towards Potocari. One wing of our army went towards Viogor, Viogor is the crest of the hill towards Milici and Srebrenica and so, God willing, we will get to Derventa from Srebrenica. This is our task. Yesterday at dusk ... "No, from Milici to Derventa. From Srebrenica to Derventa. Yes, from Srebrenica to Derventa. "Let me tell you that with yesterday's dusk any organised Muslim life to the left of the Jadar ceased existing."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, I have only one question for you in relation to this video. Did any of the mosques in Srebrenica survive the war undamaged?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- I -- none of them survived. I recognised two of the mosques referred to by Mr. Mladic in this video. One is the Petric Mahala mosque which can also be seen on the Zoran Petrovic video and for which I have formatted entry. The other one which he says is the unfinished mosque in the town square is the Carsika [phoen] mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, please remain seated. First of all I can imagine that your counsel wants to put further questions to the witness. I can imagine that. They're aware of their task and they may do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, I believe the witness may have misspoken and said it was General Mladic speaking. It is in fact General Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You shouldn't give evidence. If this witness says it is Mr. Mladic, then you can ask him if he identified Mr. Mladic. You should not tell him who was speaking, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I wasn't intending to, Your Honour, but he has identified in a transcript which has been admitted into evidence. So there is evidence that identifies the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that, but in order to test the reliability and the credibility of this witness, you should not whisper in his ear that he made a mistake and then qualify it as an error. It may be that it's misjudgement. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I hadn't intended to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I accept that you intended to do it, but you shouldn't have done it. You identified Mr. Mladic as the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a very fuzzy video. I was acting on an assumption and not as an identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't present it as an assumption. You presented it as Mr. Mladic speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you don't have to apologise. It's what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, as I say, it looks a bit like him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it means that to establish a fact requires more than some [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should have said the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I have one more clip, if we could have 65 ter 22885A. And this is a clip from a speech at the 34th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly. I'd refer Your Honours to 65 ter 02382 as well, which is the transcript of the session. This one we've provided the booth that portion of the transcript from the session, and I'd be in Your Honour's hands as to whether it's best to play it twice under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the transcript been verified before?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's a CLSS transcript of this Assembly session, but it hasn't been -- outside of the Prosecution's work it hasn't been matched up with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any need to play it twice under those circumstances or would you accept -- you can also leave it to after the first round, asking the interpreters to read the transcript, and if there's any inconsistency that we could play it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that I don't have the transcript with me right now, so it's not possible for me to compare. I have to follow either one or the other channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can provide the English page reference in that 65 ter, but I'm afraid I can't provide the B/C/S. It might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's play it twice. First round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. We have to stop it at this moment. Apparently the B/C/S volume is insufficient to follow what is said. That's at least how I interpreted your body language, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I cannot follow in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Can we put the volume up and start playing it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told there may be a problem with the volume, but it's not something that we can resolve further. It can't be turned up higher essentially than it is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this is already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The video is not. The transcript is, I believe, going to be part of our agreement with the Defence about Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a text so that you can read out the words spoken by Mr. Mladic so that we at least know what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It comes on page 72 of the English of 65 ter 02382. The clip included longer portion for context. There's only, however, one relevant sentence, and I could simply read that and forego the clip, if that suits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would suggest that you read that sentence as you say audible on this video as spoken by Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could -- it might be best I think to have page 72 of 65 ter 02382 up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's page 72 of the English. And the clip would have started with the words "Mr. President," but several lines below it includes: "We cannot allow leaving the mosques with two minarets there."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is describing an area near Tesanj as we can see slightly before that. That is not an area you have studied, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But does this perhaps clarify for you what Mr. Lukic asked you about earlier today, whether General Mladic had ever given a direction targeting a particular mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I answered Mr. Lukic, I had not seen anything like that before, but now it appears I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think given the technical difficulty with the video, it might be best simply to mark for identification the transcript of the Assembly session pending our agreement with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any objection against MFI-ing the -- if you want to consult first --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with Mr. Mladic, you have an opportunity to do so, at least if it's short and if it's not aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not object to have this document MFI'd and we can work further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number under which this document would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02382 receives number P2508, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2508 is marked for identification. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That completes my examination, Your Honour. The only remaining thing I should put on the record is that this portion of the Srebrenica trial video, P1147, the transcript began on page 60 of the English and 55 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Mr. Lukic, as the re-examination triggered any need for further questions to be asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go through the documents first. If we can see P2506 on our screens just mentioned by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Riedlmayer, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I mean before, not today during the hearing but while you were preparing for your testimony. I mean, is it the first time that you're seeing this document here today?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 4, please. [In English] I'm sorry, it's 5, and we need number 4 on page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: English, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or just in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't follow B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think it may be page 7 in the B/C/S, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here under item 4 we can see that the CSB, or rather, the police station in Sanski Most states: [In English] "Explosive devices are solely obtained from military sources ..." [Interpretation] Does this actually indicate that someone else is obtaining this material, the army would not be obtaining material from the army. Does that mean that somebody else is obtaining these explosives from these sources or perhaps you're not able to comment on this at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to comment on that. I would have to conjecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at P2507.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is also a document which was just shown to you during the redirect. Did you see this document before today?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that you cannot see from this document who it was who demolished the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document talks about the removal of the ruins. It does not talk about the actual destruction of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the mosque fell or the ruins of the mosque fell on the road and blocked it, or are you not aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it; however, having been to the site I know that the mosque was in a field set back from the road. I am also aware that at least in other trials there was some evidence presented about how the mosque was destroyed by somebody who was an eye-witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P1147, please. Perhaps Ms. Stewart could help us with this. It's the same clip at 36 minutes, 6 seconds. We just need to look at a clip from the video. We don't actually need the volume. So we just want to remind the witness what this is about. We just need to look at the image.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You remember this; right? You remember the speaker?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not go into who this is. The Prosecution did not tell you that the video was recorded on the 12th of July, and the speaker here says that the mosque was demolished. utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe from my recall here is that he's talking about two separate mosques. The Petric mosque is the one that is near the southern entrance of Srebrenica. It's not the same as the one that was discussed in my evidence, which is the market mosque in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you did not process that second one. Was it still standing when the first one that you worked on was destroyed on the 19th of July, that you can see on the frame that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know actually when it was destroyed. It was still standing in one of the Petrovic videos, but as I understand they were taken over a period of more than one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information that any of the mosques was demolished or knocked down on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an exact date of the footage of the market mosque I believe has date stamps. Some of the other footage does not. utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is the date of the Petrovic video, if you can just tell us once again for the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 13th and the 14th of July, and you can correct me if I'm wrong?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. As I said, the one of the market mosque was the 14th because it had a date stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have finished with this video and so now we need to look at the transcript in the e-court. This is 65 ter 2382 that the Prosecution showed before. We will need to look at page 72. Page 72, please, in the English version at least. [In English] Just one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we can see -- it's not clear to me what exactly this is about, but we can see that Tesanj is mentioned. So what is General Mladic talking about? However, would you agree with me that Tesanj was never held by the Army of Republika Srpska during the war, it was never under the control of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These were all my questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, just one more thing. I apologise, with the permission of the Chamber, this is not something that arises from the cross but it's my error. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would suggest that we look at the picture again and see whether any horns are visible and then ask the witness, if visible, whether that has any impact on his testimony.

utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]

utterances.text: Yes, then you came with another explanation that you just copied what that person had written down. utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would just for context refer the Chamber to the remainder of that discussion, particularly at lines 13 and 14, where the witness says: There may have been other skulls outside of the photo. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have within half a page we have two or three explanations which are all not -- I think I established already yesterday that it is not very solid and that is now confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has a question in relation to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And my question is to you, Mr. Lukic. Are you -- is it an assertion you are making that the object we see above that head is a horn?

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.text: That's an assertion you are making?

utterances.text: Okay. That at least has been clarified whether it was in response to a question, yes or no. utterances.text: We can try. I've been informed it might be a problem because it's in Sanction, but it might not.

utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's see whether it works. Could the usher assist the witness. Witness, would you please very carefully listen to my instructions as to markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see whether a technical solution can be found, if not within one or two minutes then we'll deal with it in a different way. Having read this paragraph, I observe the following and just for purposes of transparency put it on the record that the first paragraph -- the first linea of paragraph 4 deals with fewer explosions, but still be part of everyday life, mainly thrown into the yards of houses belonging to Muslims, three cases were planted in houses and facilities belonging to Serbs. The next linea deals with explosive devices solely obtained from military sources. Then in the third linea, apparently a new subject is addressed, that is, over the past two months, three mosques, having been blown up, and the kind of explosive used for blowing them up and how these explosives were transported and an accompanying shoot-out. The next linea deals with the organs of the organisation that issues this report, that the organ know some of the experts and perpetrators, some of whom are officers. And then that the organ -- organisation believes that the problem should be resolved by competent military organs and commands, especially the cases involving explosives and mines which came from army depots and combat sets of subordinate units. I put this on the record because the parties have picked each the little bits and pieces of this document and I thought that it would be good to make the parties aware that the Chamber reads this paragraph 4 on explosions in its entirety. We take a break and we'll resume at 25 past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the Chamber invites the Prosecution to call its next witness -- could Mr. Mladic speak without raising his voice. Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, the Chamber would like to deliver two decisions -- well, one of them is perhaps not a real decision. I start with delivering the decision on the Defence requests for extensions to respond to the 40th and the 41st 92 bis motions. For the second, intercept bar table motion and the bar table motion related to the Siege of Sarajevo. On the 11th of October, the Defence filed a request for a 30-day extension to respond to the Prosecution's 40th 92 bis motion, citing as good cause for the request the fact that the Prosecution has been filing its 92 bis motions at will, in direct contravention of the Chamber's guidance, as well as the concurrent dead-lines issued by the Chamber and other obligations of the Defence. The Defence also seeks clarification of the Chamber's guidance with respect to the timing of the Prosecution's filings. On the 14th of October, the Defence filed three more requests for extensions to respond: A request for 30 additional days to respond to the 41st 92 bis motion; a request for 30 additional days to respond to the second intercept bar table motion; and a request for 44 additional days to respond to the bar table motion related to the Siege of Sarajevo. The Defence cites as good cause for additional extension its current heavy workload and the complicated and serious nature of the Prosecution's bar table motions. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution's standing submission that it will not object to reasonable requests for extensions. As a preliminary matter, the Chamber notes that its original guidance with respect to the timing of 92 bis and quater motions was that the Prosecution should make such filings two or three weeks apart in order to prevent the Defence and Chamber from being flooded with these kinds of motions. However, the Chamber modified this guidance over a year ago when it stated clearly on the 12th of October, 2012, that the Prosecution could file its 92 bis and quater motions once they were ready and that the Defence could request more time if it felt that it was flooded with such motions and did not have adequate time to respond. This can be found on transcript pages 4057 to 4058. For these reasons, the Chamber finds meritless the Defence claims in relation to the 40th 92 bis motion that the Chamber's guidance has been unclear or abandoned without reason by the Chamber. With regard to the Defence submission that it was unable to respond in a timely manner to the 40th 92 bis motion because it was facing simultaneous dead-lines as a result of the Chamber's orders, the Chamber considers that there was only one other response dead-line set for the 11th of October, the response to the Prosecution's second UN bar table motion, and that dead-line was set after the Chamber granted the Defence an additional 30 days in which to respond. The Chamber also considers that the 40th 92 bis motion is brief and uncomplicated, concerning only one witness and comprising only 27 redacted transcript pages and a single photograph. With regard to the Defence request for a 30-day extension to respond to the 41st 92 bis motion, the Chamber considers that the motion is extremely brief and uncomplicated, concerning only a four-paragraph statement of a single witness. With regard to the Defence request for an extension to respond to the second intercept bar table motion, the Chamber considers that the motion is relatively brief, concerning only 13 intercepts and a small number of notebook pages. The Chamber also notes the Prosecution's submission that most of the tendered intercepts are substantially similar to those already in evidence and are only being offered to establish the date of such admitted intercepts. With respect to the Defence request for an extension to respond to the bar table motion related to the Siege of Sarajevo, the Chamber considers that the motion relates to a substantial number of documents which appear to concern, inter alia, the acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment. The Chamber recalls that its guidance with respect to the timing of Prosecution 92 bis and quater filings and the granting of reasonable requests for extensions to respond to these filings was based on its concern that the Defence not be inundated with such motions to the point where it did not have adequate time to respond. For the 40th and 41st 92 bis motions at issue, however, the Chamber does not consider that the Defence has been flooded with such motions or that the length or complexity of these motions warrant an additional 30 days to respond. With regard to the Defence's general submissions that it cannot cope with its current heavy workload, in part due to response dead-lines ordered by the Chamber, the Chamber notes that the dead-lines it has set have been a result of granting, in full or in part, the very extensions sought by the Defence. The Chamber further notes in this respect that in the last two months it has granted, in full or in part, all 16 of the Defence's requests for extensions, allowing nearly 400 additional response days. Lastly, the Chamber notes that the Defence team is staffed and funded at the highest levels afforded by the Tribunal and absent a showing of good cause the Defence is expected to keep up with the normal filings dead-lines and should not expect last-minute extensions to be granted as a matter of right where it has not shown a reasonable basis for them. For the foregoing reasons the Chamber decides as follows: For the 40th 92 bis motion: The Chamber grants the request in part, allowing an additional 14 days in which to respond and setting the new dead-line of 25th of October [Realtime transcript read in error "September"]. For the 41st 92 bis motion: The Chamber grants the request in part, allowing an additional 14 days in which to respond and setting the new dead-line of 28th of October. For the second intercept bar table motion: The Chamber grants the request, allowing an additional 30 days in which to respond, setting the new dead-line of 14 November. For the bar table motion related to the Siege of Sarajevo: The Chamber grants the request in full, allowing an additional 44 days in which to respond, setting the new dead-line of 28 November. And this concludes the Chamber's decisions.

utterances.text: I did. Well, then it only shows how exceptional mistakes by transcriptionists are, which the Chamber is always aware of that it is a difficult task. And then I would like to deal with another matter, that is the remaining evidentiary motions during the Prosecution's case. Last week, the Prosecution provided an informal update in relation to its remaining evidentiary motions to be filed during the Prosecution's case. The Chamber understands that generally no further Rule 92 bis or quater motions will be filed. In relation to bar table motions, the Chamber understands that one such motion remains to be filed and that motion will contain approximately 10 to 20 miscellaneous documents in addition to 15 excerpts of Republika Srpska Assembly sessions. This motion should be filed no later than the 31st of October. The Chamber will address the proposed further tendering of some 500 documents in a second. In relation to the proposed tendering of excerpts of RS Assembly sessions, the Chamber notes the Defence's position that it would not object if the whole sessions were tendered. The Chamber reminds the Defence that if it wishes to have certain portions added to any excerpts for contextualisation, it should request so in its response. The parties are urged to tender only excerpts or to clearly explain why entire sessions are needed. The Prosecution states in its correspondence that approximately 500 documents cited in the remaining expert reports will be tendered in the final written bar table motion because, according to the Prosecution, the Chamber has expressed its inclination to, and I quote, "restrict the Prosecution's ability to tender documents during the testimony of expert witnesses." First of all, the Chamber understands this issue to mainly refer to the documents underlying the Theunens report. Secondly, the Chamber has not expressed an inclination to restrict the Prosecution from tendering documents during the testimony of witnesses. The Chamber's guidance has always been that documents should be used with witnesses in court as opposed to tendering them from the bar table or as associated exhibits. With regard to expert witnesses, the Chamber additionally gave guidance that documents underlying expert reports should not be tendered as a matter of fact because a proposed expert report should be clear enough in relation to describing and drawing conclusions from the underlying documents, so as to make the additional tendering of certain source and underlying material unnecessary. If certain documents are not covered by the expert report, they are of course not technically underlying documents, and thus the Prosecution may tender them into evidence. The Prosecution should in such cases clearly explain why such documents are tendered. As the Chamber previously held, it is not inclined to accept a bulk of tendering of many hundreds of underlying documents, neither during the examination-in-chief nor from the bar table. The way the Prosecution should proceed is to limit its examination-in-chief, including the tendering of documents, to matters of central importance to its case which are likely to be controversial and which require further explanation, clarification, or illustration in terms of how the expert witness reached his or her conclusions or opinions. Further, as indicated at transcript page 17609, the Prosecution should analyse after the cross-examination of the expert, whether certain conclusions have been challenged by the Defence which now would require tendering of some of the underlying documents. In its correspondence in relation to Witness Tabeau, the witness states -- the Prosecution states, and I quote: "Should the Chamber find she is an expert and admit her POD expert report, it's not the Prosecution's intention, as a general rule, to tender documents related to victims which are not specifically challenged by the Mladic Defence. Absent a specific challenge, the Prosecution considers tendering the underlying documents may, in most cases, be unnecessary." Based on this, the Chamber understands that the Prosecution will proceed in accordance with the Chamber's guidance with respect to Witness Tabeau. With regard to the Prosecution's reference to wanting to tender 2.000 documents with Witness Tabeau, the Chamber then understands that this is only so if the Defence specifically challenges the expert's finding in relation to each victim. The Prosecution did not give a similar indication that it will proceed in accordance with the Chamber's guidance for other expert witnesses; however, the Chamber expects the Prosecution to do so. The Prosecution also sought guidance on the Chamber's approach to evaluating the evidence alluding -- to evaluate the evidence alluding to a verification process conducted by the Stanisic and Zupljanin Trial Chamber. The Chamber cannot at this stage provide any clarification on how it will evaluate the evidence, once received, and whether it will engage in a similar exercise as the mentioned Trial Chamber. In terms of assisting the Prosecution in its determination of what material should be tendered, the Chamber considers that the instant statement serves as sufficient guidance. Lastly, the Prosecution requested that a Rule 65 ter meeting be held to help clarify what issues related to Witness Tabeau's report are in dispute. While the Chamber always encourages the parties to meet and clarify what matters are in dispute, it is not inclined to get involved in this -- these meetings at this stage. In addition, whether something is challenged or not will further only crystalise during cross-examination. And this concludes this statement by the Chamber. If the Prosecution is ready, the next witness could be called, that's Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy Bowen has worked as a war correspondent for the British Broadcasting Corporation since 1987. In this capacity, he has reported on wars in the former Yugoslavia, beginning with the war in Croatia, before being stationed in Sarajevo from July 1992 for the majority of the conflict in Bosnia. In Sarajevo he observed that there was no safe place from the campaign of shelling and sniping against the civilian population. Mr. Bowen spoke to Bosnian Serb soldiers who were encircling Sarajevo, who confirmed that they were firing into the city. Mr. Bowen also reported from areas outside of Sarajevo. In August 1992, he accompanied a UNHCR convoy into Gorazde, where he witnessed desperate people suffering from a lack of food and medical supplies. He also witnessed the effects of shelling. He also reported on ethnic cleansing of Bosnian Muslim civilians from various locations throughout Bosnia, which he describes as a major and constant feature of the conflict. In July 1995, Mr. Bowen reported on events in Srebrenica and recalls pointing out that in the pictures he took from Pale TV, no men were shown leaving the enclave. That concludes the summary of the written evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you arrived in Sarajevo in July 1992, and for the first half of the examination today we'll focus on your experiences in Sarajevo between 1992 and 1995. Now, in your written statement, P2515 MFI, you mention that you got to know a refugee family who was sheltering in the hotel Europa in Sarajevo, in connection with this I would like to show you one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Stewart will now play 65 ter 22510M and this is a clip that has been previewed by CLSS and therefore I hope to play it only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the transcript been provided --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
