utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The fire was started by four shells which hit the hotel Europa around 7.00 last night. It took hold rapidly engulfing the top floors of the building. More than 800 refugees were in the hotel. Most of them were women and children, most came from suburbs of Sarajevo now controlled by the Serbs. They've already lost their homes and almost all of their possessions. As the fire spread through the hotel, they grabbed what they had left and tried to get out. The shelling has forced most of the refugees to spend every night in the basement. This city has hundreds of thousands of defenceless people, but the refugees are as vulnerable as anybody here. They filed out to what they thought was the safety of the street, but snipers started shooting as they came out. Passers-by tried to take people out of the firing line. Someone managed to get a few vans to evacuate them from the most immediate danger. But it's all relative, there's no such thing as a safe place in this city. This morning this was all that was left of the top floor. Until last night it passed as home for scores of refugees. Small fires are still burning in the roof, downstairs the refugees are moving back in. They don't want to, but there's nowhere else left. "This woman said her house had been destroyed, she didn't know where to go or what to do. This young mother is just as dazed, she came to the hotel three days ago because her brother had been killed by a mortar and it seemed safe, now she doesn't know whether to stay or to go. The refugees believe the Serbs attacked their hotel deliberately. "I don't know, they attacked us because they knew we are here. "The 'Europa' is in the old quarter of Sarajevo, an area which has been mortared hundreds of times by the Serbs, whose positions are very close. "Any denials coming from the Serbian side should be treated with the greatest skepticism. Once again it seems the gunners on the hills around here are treating civilians not just as legitimate targets but as their main enemy."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we've paused the clip at 2.28 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, at the start of the clip there was a black introduction screen that contained the date 11 June 1992. Was that, in fact, a date of this footage?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. I'd ignore that. In those days we didn't have the technology, the software, when we were moving around in the field to change the dates on the countdowns. We of course do now, but back then if you were outside the head office, you couldn't make those changes. So in general in all of these reports, I would ignore the dates on that lead-in because most of the time they're not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you recall the approximate date of this footage?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It would have been in July 1992 I'm pretty certain.

utterances.text: And in the footage I noticed a few men carrying weapons. Do you know whether the hotel Europa was at the time being used for a military purpose?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I saw no evidence of that. I got to know the hotel pretty well after that, because as you said, I got to know a refugee family there who I actually befriended and used to -- they'd tell me what was going on and I used to give them food and things and coffee. And so I never ever saw any sign of it being used as any kind of a military headquarters throughout the war because people moved back in as you saw in that piece. It was used as a place where displaced people, where refugees, were staying. The men with guns were, I think, various fighters who'd come in to help out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can continue playing the clip, please, to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "On the other side of the city, nearly a thousand people, mainly mothers and children, became refugees this morning. Almost all of them were Serbs. Until the war started, they'd lived happily enough alongside Muslims and Croats. "Horrible, horrible. I have to go. This is my town, I'm born here, and my child born here, and my father living here. I have to leave everything. "Misery is about the only thing the ordinary people of the former Yugoslavia still have in common. "Jeremy Bowen, BBC news, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, in the second half of this clip, we saw you reporting on Bosnian Serbs leaving Sarajevo. Were they leaving from government-controlled areas of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in this clip we see you reporting from both the Bosnian Muslim perspective and the Bosnian Serb perspective. Was this intentional or incidental to the report?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: It was always very important to us to try to report from all sides of the conflict of the war. It wasn't always possible, but we -- we did the best that we could in the circumstances, to try to report every side. Now, I was especially keen to report from the Serb side, but it was very difficult to get access to places which they controlled. It was particularly difficult to get, for example, Grbavica, which was, as you know, the part of central Sarajevo which was controlled by the Serb side. And despite asking many, many times of the Serb authorities, Bosnian Serb authorities, in Pale, I think I managed in the course of the whole war to visit there once. Only once did I get permission to go there, and you had to have permission to get in because it was controlled by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you recall the details of the circumstances of the departure of the Bosnian Serbs from government-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I believe - and it's more than 20 years ago now - but I believe that what was happening was it was an evacuation that was organised and there were mainly Serbs on the bus because the bus going to head towards Serbia. I think at that time a lot of people were getting out because of the circumstances of the war. I think that in July 1992, while there was probably already a little bit of pressure on Serbs there, it wasn't anything like it got to be later on in the war because there -- still the people talked a lot still in Sarajevo at that time of a multi-cultural ethos. So my -- to the best of my memory, these were people who were getting out because it was dangerous and were unhappy to have to leave because of the danger and feeling that they were being driven out of their homes by the war.

utterances.text: P2517 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, in the clip we just saw, you observed that Serb gunners were not just treating civilians as their legitimate targets, but as their main enemy. In connection with this comment, I'd like to show you another of your reports. This is 65 ter 22510D, and it's the shelling of the graveyard that you reported on and you've already mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "No one bothered to tell Svetlana Glavas and her mother Ruza that Svetlana's daughter was being sent to Germany. No one in authority bothered to tell them that she'd been killed either. A neighbour who'd heard about Vedrana's murder on the radio broke the news. This morning as they got ready to go to the funeral, they said that Vedrana lived at the children's home because they couldn't look after her properly in their tiny damp flat. They said they loved Vedrana though, her grandmother kept one of Svetlana's dolls for her. Vedrana was two and a half, and they went to see her as often as they could. "She had just begun to walk, she couldn't talk yet. But she could play with a ball. "Svetlana and Ruza had planed to walk to the graveyard with their neighbours. But it's at least two miles from where they lived, so with our colleagues from the Reuters News Agency, we gave them a lift. When they arrived they were told that Vedrana had already been buried, half an hour early because the graveyard was being shelled by the Serbs. That was bad enough but it got much worse. More shells started falling. One landed as the boys and girls from Vedrana's children's home arrived with their flowers. As quickly as they could they dropped them on the graves of Vedrana and the baby boy the sniper also murdered. It was time to go. As the family was leaving, the gunners found their range. "Ruza Glavas, the grandmother, was hit in the arm. Reporters tried to stop the bleeding. "Hurry up! Another dressing! Tourniquet, tourniquet! Tight, tight, tight! Get the woman's daughter! "Another shell exploded as she was carried to the car. "Her daughter! "The doctors said they could save Ruza's arm but that she might lose the use of it. She tried to tell her daughter that she was all right. Svetlana is educationally subnormal and very dependent of her. "At least six mortar rounds landed in or around the graveyard. There were two direct hits just at the time that the children's funerals were due to start. The shooting isn't always this accurate, but the place is attacked every day. There is no question that the Serb gunners are targeting the graveyard to kill civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, the man in the cream trousers and the blue shirt and flak jacket that we saw attending to Ruza Glavas, the lady that had been shot, was that you?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record, that's at minute 1.57 of the clip that we just watched.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, do you have any particular comment that you would like to make about this clip, about your recollection of this experience?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- to start with as a human being, I was absolutely outraged by what had happened that day. I thought it was despicable. Killing two children was bad enough, shooting them when they were being evacuated on a very badly organised evacuation mission, but then shelling their funeral, I just thought it was grotesque. Wounding the grandmother, she had a serious wound in her arm, a bill hole, as my colleague Kurt Shaw, and my other colleague who was there who was a doctor, Jasmina Alabegovic, treating her, the big field dressings went right into the hole. I mean, it disappeared into there. It was such a big hole in her arm. You could see the distress of the daughter who was a very needy woman. So I was -- to start with, I was outraged by what had happened. Second of all, what I got from talking to grave-diggers and to witnesses and to people who were at the cemetery every day, was that it was a regular occurrence, that the graveyard would be shelled quite often. In fact, it's dominated by a large stone lion, and during the war years, I think it's been repaired now, but during the war years that lion was very badly chipped and pitted because of the amount of shrapnel that had been thrown off by detonations near it in the funeral. So, you know, one of the things I wanted to find out was: Was there any chance this might be being done for our benefit because we were there as TV cameras. And overwhelmingly what I got that day and on previous visits as well and on subsequent visits to that very cemetery - I went there quite a bit - was that shelling was a regular occurrence when TV cameras were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you say -- do those comments that you have just provided provide the basis for the comment that you make in your statement -- sorry, in the clip that we just saw, saying: "There's no question that the Serb gunners were targeting the graveyard to kill civilians"?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, there was a clear line of sight from the graveyard, which is on a raised positions, it's up a hill, in Sarajevo to the hills where Serb army military positions were. I'm very well aware of the conspiracy theories that the Bosnian government side were shelling themselves and shelling their own people and those were being stated even more or less at that time. But I never found any evidence of that happening. The evidence that day seemed to be that the fire was coming from the Serb side -- actually, in the course of my time in Sarajevo, I would have been absolutely delighted to report the story that the Bosnian army was shelling its own people, Bosnian government army was shelling its own people. Because as a -- you know, as an impartial journalist, I'm keen to report every side and I wouldn't have hesitated in reporting that story if we had found any evidence; we never did. And I'm encouraged in my belief 20 years on that my call that day was correct because in all the years since then nobody has come forward and said: Yes, I did it. You'd think that after this amount of time it would be very hard to keep that kind of thing hidden and it hasn't -- it's never emerged to my knowledge anyway. So that day, yes, it seemed to be that there was already a pattern that artillery positions on the Serb side were targeting the graveyard in a way that they also targeted other parts of the city, it has to be said. And, you know, shelling was -- was -- it's -- was the daily drum beat there. You know, you heard shelling almost all of the time in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender that clip as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22510D receives number P2518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, in paragraph 44 of your statement, you refer to a report that you made on the shelling of a football game in Dobrinja. We've already looked at that paragraph today when you clarified the date was, in fact, June 1993 rather than July. This is an incident that is charged in our indictment as shelling incident G4, and I'd like to show you that footage now, 65 ter 22510A.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this has been admitted into evidence through RM123, pursuant to the Chamber's 24th 92 bis filing on the 2nd of April. I don't think we've yet had an exhibit number assigned to it, but it is -- it is in evidence. And I would also note that this isn't a clip that was provided to CLSS in advance but it is already in evidence and that was the reason why we didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can you confirm that it has not yet been assigned an exhibit number, although apparently been admitted -- having been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It was admitted pursuant to your decision on the 3rd of October, 2013, transcript page 19974 to 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a recent decision, therefore, which may explain why it has not yet been assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that Madam Registrar has not received yet a message that everything that needed to be uploaded was uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and that will be coming this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you reserve a number for it, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The reserved number for document 22510A will be P2519, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that will be marked for identification for the time being -- no, it's -- it should -- it's admitted already, although not in the system yet. So therefore, I'm a bit hesitant what to do at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number is assigned now and it will be dealt with by Madam Registrar in the near future when assigning numbers to other exhibits that were admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we please play the clip, Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "Just after the attack an amateur cameraman went with the wounded to the clinic in Dobrinja. Several hundred men, women, and children were watching football when the first shell landed. A second exploded a few minutes later, wounding people who'd gone to help victims of the first. "Today we had a very, very sick, a very bad day. A lot of injured patients, a lot of injured civilians and children. What can I say now for all world, for civilisation? "Dobrinja is one of the most violent places in Sarajevo. They're used to shelling, but the make-shift pitch is surrounded by high blocks of flats and they thought the Serbs wouldn't be able to see them. The people here just wanted to have some fun. Today is one of the most important Muslim festivals of the year, and a game of football was the only way they had to celebrate it. 'We can't live like animals forever,' one of them said, 'after all, we are human beings.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, do you recognise this as the report that you filed on the shelling of the football game in Dobrinja in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we're at the break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're at break time. Mr. Jeremy, could you give us an indication, if we would resume at ten minutes to 2.00, would you then come to your 70 minutes or ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I won't conclude before 2.15. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom and we'll resume at ten minutes to 2.00.

utterances.text: We take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just while the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jeremy. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just while the witness is being brought in, the next clip I'm going to play is 22879G, and just to mention that the transcript of this clip hasn't been provided to the booth; however, the transcript of a longer version of the same clip, 22879E has been and the corrections have been made, and, therefore, on that basis I propose to only play 22879G once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, although I note I think two numbers have been identified. I think -- oh, I see, no objections. We're fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And to be clear, Your Honours, the booths have transcripts of both clips, but they've only pre-verified the transcript of the longer clip and, therefore, their corrections to that transcript is [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you guide them where the shorter clip is in the larger clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's -- it's under a separate 65 ter 22879G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, in the first of the reports that we viewed today, you stated that -- and that report was in July 1992, one of the first reports you did on your arrival into Sarajevo, you stated that "there was no such thing as a safe place in the city." Now, this was in 1992. Did the city become safer after that time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: No, it didn't. The thing that characterised the government-held part of Sarajevo, the bulk of the centre of the city of course at that time was that there was really -- there was nowhere where you couldn't get shelled and there were many places where you could get sniped. So there was nowhere safe really in the city out in the open, and in the course of the war, right up to the summer of 1995 when I was still there, that didn't change.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another of your reports now, 22879G.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "This is as dangerous and unstable as Sarajevo has been since the war started more than three years ago. Another improvised Serb rocket hit a block of flats. Three more people were killed. Serb attacks against civilian targets are escalating steadily. In the last ten days or so more than 50 civilians have been killed and scores of others injured. "Jeremy Bowen, BBC news, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, do you recall the approximate date of that clip?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it's around July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in the clip you referred to another improvised Serb rocket. Can you explain what you meant by improvised Serb rocket?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, to -- well, to start with, that incident followed on from an attack on the TV station which is more or less in the same time-period which is why I said "another." And by improvised, by the information that we were getting was that there were rockets which had been designed for another purpose but which were being -- they improvised ways of using them as a ground attack weapon and they were powerful which was why when they hit that building people were killed and also the building you just saw, and also when one hit the TV station there was also a lot of damage and some injuries too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender that clip as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P2520, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2520 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, in paragraph 24 of your statement you state: "The dead and wounded in Sarajevo were not caught in the cross-fire between two warring armies. Instead, between 1992 and 1995 they were subjected to an organised campaign of shelling and sniping by Bosnian Serb forces encircling the city." Now, this is rather a strong statement. Can you provide the basis for your making of this particular statement?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Sure. The confrontation lines barely changed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry about that. The confrontation lines didn't -- I'm getting the B/C/S now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if we move on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it will be better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- it will go away. The confrontation lines didn't really changed except in one or two places in the course of the -- of the entire 1992 to 1995 period. So in other words, what I'm saying is there was a war going on between the two sides and they all knew where each other's positions were. But consistently, throughout the war, there were attacks which seemed to me to be sometimes targeted and sometimes pretty random on the city. You know, you'd be driving along -- and I saw with my own eyes shells exploding, hitting buildings in -- in parts of the centre of the city. And that's what made me believe that they weren't caught in the cross-fire because people clearly didn't live in the places where there were military positions, they'd moved out of those. But there were right through the war and we filmed it, there was other photographic evidence, I saw it, I saw civilians lying on streets, in the centre of Sarajevo, with -- killed through with sniper rounds to the head. I -- there was right next to the Holiday Inn where we stayed, the Holiday Inn hotel where the journalists stayed, there was a bit of open ground, in fact, it was the car park of the hotel and now is the car park again, but then it was abandoned because there was a direct line of sight into Bosnian Serb positions which were only a few hundred yards away, maybe 400, 500 yards maybe. And I remember once being in the restaurant looking out, as I'm having my lunch I'm looking out and I saw a man trying to cross that ground, people would sprint across it and he was hit in the leg and he fell over and I actually went down to the garage of the hotel and got my armoured Land Rover and drove it out to try to pick him up because when I -- I could see him lying there. By the time I got there, only a couple of minutes later he had dragged himself away. And that was typical. And also I saw many, many civilian casualties and I spoke to many, many civilians who talk about being in their homes having breakfast with their families and then the place would be shelled and people would get killed. One of our translators had a tank shell going through her parents' apartment. Luckily it didn't explode and so nobody was hurt. But it went right through it from the front window to the back window. You know, and I could go on. And also I spent -- I was a regular visitor to the morgue in -- the morgue at Kosevo hospital because it was very hard to get accurate casualty figures and one of the ways that we did it was to go and count bodies ourselves and I could tell when there was activity on front lines because you'd see they'd put the bodies in there, they wouldn't strip them, they'd just be in their clothes. And you could see men in military uniforms when there was fighting going on around the city, but at other times there would be elderly women there or children or sniper victims with head wounds and chest wounds. So that's what -- it was really the evidence which I saw with my own eyes over three years which made me say that I felt it was an organised campaign of shelling and sniping. It didn't -- it happened so often, it could not possibly have been coincidental. There was an intelligence behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to your evidence relating to ethnic cleansing, and in paragraph 9 of your statement you -- you say that you learned about ethnic cleansing in Bosnia because you saw it happening. Now, can you provide the Chamber with the working definition that you apply when using this expression "ethnic cleansing."

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, by "ethnic cleansing," I mean the forcible eviction of people from their homes, from their villages, from their towns, and their deportation, again always -- often but not always at gunpoint deportation, and that was happening on grounds of their ethnicity. In other words, they were being kicked out of their homes by force because they were from the wrong ethnic group, with the intention of trying to create an ethnically pure area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph -- in your statement in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In 1992 in central and Western Bosnia in your written evidence, you provide news reports on Bosnian Muslim refugees, overwhelmingly women and children, that you observed arriving in Travnik, in Karlovac, from a number of different municipalities in Western Bosnia. You also reported from Trnopolje camp and your words from this report are included in your Karadzic testimony, now in evidence as P2516, MFI. At transcript page T10097 you state: "As far as hard-line concerns -- Serbs are concerned, a camp like this is a success for the policy of ethnic cleansing." Can you explain the basis for your belief why in 1992 there was a successful policy of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Well, I said it was a success by its own lights, by it's -- the intentions of the people who framed the policy because a very large number of people were expelled from their homes and the process of changing the ethnic balance was -- was going ahead. And that, therefore, was for them a success. It meant that people who they didn't want to have near them were being moved out, forcibly, and that men who were of military age were being put into detention camps, where presumably the reasons -- one of the reasons for that were quite obvious, they didn't want to push over men of military age into Bosnian-government-controlled territory where they could be taken on by the army and carry a gun against the people who had kicked them out of their homes. I saw, for example, in Travnik large numbers, in the thousands, of Muslim people being -- who were arriving there who had been expelled from their homes and there were the vast -- well, all of -- there were no young men. They all -- all the women and the older men there came out with the same stories about young men, men of fighting age, and boys as well, teenagers, being taken away and separated away from them and taken off. So yeah, ethnic cleansing was happening on a scale that to me it seemed clear that it was happening under orders. It wasn't happening spontaneously. And so therefore, there was a political, strategic intention behind it. And I said it was a success story because it was happening and nothing was being -- nothing was happening to stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Moving to -- from central and Western Bosnia to Eastern Bosnia, you went to Gorazde as part of a UNHCR convoy in 1992, and you discuss this in your statement and we don't need to discuss that further now. But still in Eastern Bosnia and moving to 1993 in Cerska, you were again part of a UNHCR convoy that was trying to gain access to Cerska. And in your statement, paragraph 63, you describe passing through a series of roadblocks before being stopped by Bosnian Serb military personnel in Zvornik. You state in paragraph 64: "As it turned out, we ended up staying on the side of the road for three or four nights while the Serbs busied themselves taking over Cerska." Now, in connection with this I'd like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we see 65 ter 01027. This is a letter from the European Community Monitoring Mission to General Mladic dated 2 March 1993 regarding the treatment of the Bosnian Muslim population in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, referring to the document on the screen before you in paragraph 1 in the second sentence we see the words: "Although promises have been made to allow regular humanitarian aid into the pockets no progress has so far been made to improve the situation for the suffering of the civilian population." In paragraph 7 goes on to say: "We strongly urge you to allow the planned convoys free and safe passage into the pockets, where the population is desperately needing food." Now, do the letters that I -- do the words that I've read out from this letter to General Mladic comport with your own experience of trying to gain access to Cerska during a similar sort of time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can absolute corroborate from my own personal, on-the-ground experience that that was happening. I went with the UNHCR convoy, which was protected by people from UNPROFOR by men from the French Foreign Legion, to -- which we were -- they were intending to get to Cerska and we were stopped in Zvornik for a few days until they gave up and turned around because we went there not on -- not speculatively. We went there because the UNHCR - and I was -- I had a very good relationship with the man who was in charge of the convoy, Larry Hollingworth, the UNHCR had had assurances from the Bosnian Serb side that they would be allowed to get into Cerska. In fact, Larry had said to me: You should come along because I'm absolutely certain that we can get in. We've had cast-iron assurances from the Serb side that we will be able to get into Cerska. So why don't you come just as you came to Gorazde last year. So that's why I was with them on their particular mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you mention in paragraph 67 of your statement that you were able to eventually gain access to Cerska and you do provide some details about what you were able to view once you did. My question is: Were you able to see any Bosnian Muslim civilians in Cerska once you gained access?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: What struck me very strongly when we were finally by -- allowed just after that period, allowed by the Bosnian Serb army to go to Cerska was -- well, there's a couple of things. First of all, Cerska isn't one place. It's an area with a number of hamlets within it. And what's -- really struck me. I thought to myself: Well, where have all the people gone? Where are the people? Because the place was empty. It had become a ghost town. There was no sign of any sort of habitation. The Bosnian Serb officers who were with us took us to a mass grave that was being exhumed, it had, I think, a few bodies in, and they said that these were people from their side who'd been killed by the Muslim side, as they called it. Some of the UNPROFOR people and UNHCR people who I was with said that there was also evidence that these people had been killed in fighting, looking at the kind of bodies that there were and the sort of wounds that they had. But the Bosnian Serb side claimed strongly that their people had been tortured, subjected to atrocities, and they had had to step in to try to put an end to all of this. But, you know, equally there were no civilians; they'd all gone. So there was no one there for me to talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And at the time, did you have any idea about where those Bosnian Serb civilians who were in Cerska had gone? Did anyone make you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well the assumption -- the assumption was that they had fallen back towards Srebrenica, that the pocket there, the enclave, was getting more and more people coming in from outlying places like Cerska and in other words that the front line was shrinking back. And so they were going into that particular area. So as it turned out, in fact, quite a few of the people that were in Srebrenica had already been displaced from other parts of Eastern Bosnia in the course of the war because of the military pressure of the Bosnian Serb army and its various auxiliaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would next move to a video, but perhaps it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's better --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- we could do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an estimate on how much time you would still need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I've used 55 minutes, Your Honours, and I think I will need to use the full one hour, ten minutes that I requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So another --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another 15 minutes. Then we will adjourn, but not until after I have instructed you, Mr. Bowen, not to speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you gave today or whether it's testimony still to be given tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.
